paper_title: TTB: Test-time Baking for Efficient Rendering of Decoder-only View Synthesis Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Decoder-only Large View Synthesis Models (LVSMs) with KV-cache have recently achieved state-of-the-art quality by regressing novel views from neural networks without reconstructing 3D geometry, while Test-Time Training (TTT) layers save computation but sacrifice quality. We propose Test-Time Baking (TTB), a strategy that learns to bake global scene information from cross-view attention into a lightweight MLP, enabling fast and high-fidelity novel-view decoding. The first key is to repurpose the fast-weight MLP of TTT to learn the cross-view attention mapping explicitly from its input-output pairs, rather than replacing attention entirely, achieving the same rendering efficiency as TTT while delivering substantially higher quality. The second key addresses a modality misalignment between context prefilling and novel-view rendering: we disentangle context tokens into camera-only context rendering tokens to serve as TTB input, and context ground-truth tokens with image content to serve as the TTB mapping target, ensuring the baked MLPs are relieved of the modality generalization challenge between context and novel-view processing. Our method achieves up to **23x** rendering speedup with quality on par with the state-of-the-art across several benchmarks. Project page: https://test-time-baking.github.io

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Our research studies the task of novel-view synthesis conditioned on set of context images with the powerful Large View Synthesis Models (LVSMs) [25]. LVSMs have recently emerged with several immediate follow-up improvements [22, 31, 58, 69, 77], achieving state-of-the-art novel-view synthesis quality across various input conditions [1, 23, 42, 64]. Their geometry-free scene representations and Transformer-based renderers are fully learning-based, making them favorable for scaling with increasing amounts of training data. The minimized 3D inductive bias also shows advantages when scenes are challenging for existing Transformer-compatible geometry-based representations (e.g., 3DGS [29]), such as surfaces with strong mirror reflections or translucent material. We are especially interested in the decoder-only variant of LVSM [25] for its high-fidelity. DVSM [58] further introduces KV-cache to the cross-view attention layers, showing both quality and efficiency improvement. The KV-cache serves as global scene state for novel-view queries, but the rendering time is still impractical under dense context view conditions due to the linear complexity per token when attending to the KV-cache. LaCT [77] takes different approach by replacing cross-view attention layers with Test-Time Training (TTT) [59] layers, as illustrated in Fig. 2a. TTT performs inner-loop optimization to adapt fast-weight MLPs [49] to directly map queries to their values without the quadratic-complexity attention, which can also be interpreted as variant of linear attention [36]. Despite achieving constant-complexity rendering speed, TTT significantly sacrifices rendering quality. naive remedy for LaCT is to initialize from pretrained decoder-only model weights, which does improve quality, but the gap to the pretrained model remains significant. We argue that this quality gap can be minimized by repurposing the fast-weight MLP inner-loop optimization as baking the information from cross-view attention, rather than replacing cross-view attention entirely as in TTT. We dub our strategy Test-Time Baking (TTB), illustrated in Fig. 2b. The key motivation is to trade context-view processing time for faster and higher-fidelity novel-view rendering, achieving the Pareto frontier of quality and speed shown in Fig. 1. Specifically, the inner-loop learning target becomes the output tokens from cross-view attention, instead of the raw value tokens used in TTT. This formulation also generalizes beyond the linear-attention interpretation of TTT [36]. In principle, the learning target of our TTB can also be tokens from arbitrarily non-linear layers or tokens enriched with additional scene information. Furthermore, we identify modality misalignment issue inherent to the context prefilling of MLP fast-weight for novel-view synthesis. In the reconstruction stage (context prefilling), the fast-weight MLPs are updated using context tokens with both camera and image information. In the rendering stage, however, the updated MLPs take novel-view tokens coming from camera-only input without any image content. This conventional pipeline poses reconstruction-rendering input modality misalignment challenge. 2 Our solution to modality misalignment is simple yet effective. As illustrated in Fig. 2c, we pair each context view into i) context ground-truth tokens, derived from input cameras and images that produce the global scene information to be baked, and ii) context rendering tokens, derived from camera-only input that simulates novel-view rendering conditions. At each TTB layer, the fast-weight MLP is optimized to map context rendering tokens to their corresponding context ground-truth tokens, which carry image and cross-view attended information. The optimized TTB-MLP is then shared between context rendering tokens and the downstream novel-view rendering tokens for retrieving scene information, ensuring that their conditioning remains identical across all layers. Interestingly, TTB draws natural parallel with traditional implicit radiance and light field reconstruction, where MLPs are optimized to map spatial coordinates to radiance values. In TTB, the fast-weight MLP instead is optimized to map ray-patch latent coordinates to their appearance latent representations, which effectively performs few-step light-field optimization in latent space. This perspective suggests that TTB interpolates appearance latents for novel viewpoints from their ray-patch latent coordinates, motivating convergence-oriented inner loop over one-shot summarization. In summary, our contributions are as follows: We propose Test-Time Baking, which retargets the inner-loop optimization of the TTT fastweight MLP from raw value tokens to cross-view attention outputs, so that the fast-weight MLP collaborates with attention rather than replacing it. We identify modality misalignment between the reconstruction and rendering stages of MLP fast-weight prefilling, and resolve it via context pair that disentangles each context view into ground-truth and camera-only rendering token. We draw connection between TTBs inner loop and light field optimization in latent space, which motivates convergence-oriented training recipe (multi-step MSE) that we find particularly effective for TTB.

sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: Per-Scene optimization. Early approaches to novel-view synthesis perform per-scene optimization, fitting differentiable scene representations to observed images via differentiable rendering. Coordinatebased MLPs [2, 4, 41], voxels [8, 15, 34, 43, 56, 57], and the landmark 3DGS [29] as the scene representation have been widely explored. Despite impressive quality, per-scene optimization does not scale with the increasing training scenes and degrades quickly under fewer input views. Geometry-based feed-forward models. To overcome the scalability limitations and lengthy procedure of per-scene optimization, learning-based methods train networks to predict 3D representations from images. Early works estimated multi-plane images via cost volumes [16, 17, 40, 68, 72, 73], while NeRF-based generalizable methods [7, 37, 67, 74] extended coverage to wide-angle viewpoints at limited quality. The advent of 3DGS [29] reframed the problem as pixel-aligned GS prediction [6, 10, 24, 60, 62, 71], achieving promising results, and Large Reconstruction Models (LRMs) [21] further demonstrated Transformer scalability across various 3D representations [5, 70, 76]. One fundamental limitation of handcrafted 3D is their degradation on surfaces or materials they are not designed for, whereas the geometry-free representations we study can learn them given data. Furthermore, explicit 3D geometry lacks compact latent representation, and efforts to manage their linearly growing output size under more input views [11, 12, 45, 63] remain symptom of this constraint. Our TTB bakes scenes into constant-size MLPs at higher quality. Geometry-free feed-forward models. An alternative paradigm sidesteps the limitations of geometrybased models by representing scenes as latent representations and rendering via neural networks. Early methods [13, 46, 47, 53, 54, 55] were constrained by limited network capacity, while Large View Synthesis Models (LVSMs) [25] broke this barrier by leveraging powerful Transformers. Encoder-decoder and decoder-only LVSM variants are explored. The encoder-decoder LVSM [25] encodes context views into scene tokens and decodes novel views conditioned on the encoded scene, with subsequent works refining scene encoding strategies [22, 31, 69] and extending to generative [1] and uncalibrated camera [23, 42, 64, 78] settings. The decoder-only LVSM [25], on the other hand, uses single network for both context prefilling and novel-view rendering. Despite higher fidelity, its original form inefficiently processes context views independently for each novel view. DVSM [58] addresses this by prefilling context views into KV-cache shared across all novel views, achieving 3 Figure 3: Pipeline. Our model stacks identical blocks of Intra-view Attention, FFN, Test-Time Baking, and FFN. In the reconstruction stage, each context view is duplicated into context pair, where the context ground-truth token (ctx-gt) carries RGB and pose while the context rendering token (ctx-rend) is pose-only and matches the modality of the novel rendering token (nv). At each TTB layer, the inner-loop update bakes the fast-weight MLP via MSE loss to map (ctx-rend) toward the cross-view attention output of (ctx-gt). The baked MLP is applied to serve three token streams: it propagates both (ctx-rend) and (nv) to the next layer, and provides feedback to (ctx-gt) as an auxiliary signal. In the novel-view rendering stage, each token retrieves global scene information in O(1) from the baked MLP, instead of O(N ) via cross-attention. The rendering loss is backpropagated through the inner-loop baking process to train the model end-to-end. state-of-the-art quality under both sparse and dense view settings. However, the linearly growing KVcache size makes rendering speed impractical for larger numbers of input views. LaCT [77] replaces cross-view attention with Test-Time Training layers to achieve constant rendering complexity, but at significant quality cost compared to DVSM. Our Test-Time Baking achieves the same constant rendering complexity while substantially closing the quality gap left by LaCT. Test-time Training layers. TTT [59] has recently emerged as popular alternative to attention for its linear time and constant space complexity. We refer interested readers to [36] for an in-depth review and analysis. We are particularly interested in the variant presented in LaCT [77], which has demonstrated success in accelerating various vision and 3D tasks [9, 14, 18, 26, 63], albeit at the cost of quality relative to their attention-based counterparts. Our TTB departs from this paradigm in two ways: rather than replacing attention, TTB learns directly from attention outputs; and rather than performing mere token-to-token information exchange, TTB explicitly learns to map camera-ray tokens to their corresponding image tokens, yielding improved novel-view synthesis quality.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: We start by formally introducing our task and the general pipeline in Sec. 3.1. We detail the decoderonly architecture we build on in Sec. 3.2. Finally, we present Test-Time Baking in Sec. 3.3.

sections.title: 3.1 Overview
sections.content: Given set of context images with known poses and intrinsics {Ii RHW 3, Pi SE(3), Ki R33}V i=1, our goal is to synthesize novel views for an arbitrary camera query (P, K). We focus on reconstruction rather than generation, assuming novel views can be directly regressed from the context views. Approaches to this end generally decompose into two stages: = Recon(I, P, K), = Rend(P, K, S), (1) where Recon() processes context views into method-specific scene representation S, and Rend() synthesizes the novel view conditioned on S. Recent feed-forward models instantiate Recon() as Transformer. The Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) [21] family employs human-defined 3D and renderer, while the Large View Synthesis Model (LVSM) [25] series defines as latent state and implements Rend() as neural network. As both Recon() and Rend() are differentiable, models are trained end-to-end against ground-truth novel views by: = MSE(I, I) + λ Percep(I, I) , (2) where Percep is the neural perceptual loss [27] and λ balances the photometric objectives.

sections.content: Our method builds on the Decoder-only View Synthesis Model (DVSM) [58], which uses shared Transformer decoder for both Recon() and Rend(), and represents the scene as KV caches. Specifically, the model consists of repeated blocks, each comprising sequence of layers: Xℓ = (FFNℓ,2 CrossAttnℓ FFNℓ,1 IntraAttnℓ)(Xℓ1) , (3) where IntraAttn() and CrossAttn() perform intra-view and cross-view attention, respectively, and FFN() denotes fully connected layer. During rendering, novel-view tokens query the cached KV to retrieve global scene information from each CrossAttn() layer. sections.title: 3.3 Test-time Baking
sections.content: We present our technical contribution to improve the rendering-time efficiency of DVSM [58] while retaining its high rendering quality. The issue of DVSM is that its KV-cache size grows linearly with the number of context tokens, making it slow and impractical for novel-view queries under high-resolution or dense input context views. naive strategy is to replace each CrossAttn() in Eq. 3 with Test-Time Training (TTT) [59] layer, achieving constant space and linear time complexity as demonstrated in LaCT [77]. However, we observe significant quality degradation even when finetuning the TTT variant from DVSM pretrained weights. This motivates us to explore better solution that improves upon TTT. full model pipeline is illustrated in Fig. 3.

sections.title: 3.3.1 Repurposing TTT: collaborating instead of replacing attention
sections.content: Our motivation is to trade reconstruction (prefilling) computation, which only needs to be performed once per scene, for improved rendering-time speed and quality. The resulting solution is simple yet effective. Rather than entirely replacing cross-view attention with TTT fast-weight MLP as in the LaCT [77], we repurpose TTT to explicitly learn from the input-output pairs out of cross-view attention. Consequently, we no longer need to cache the KV; only the updated MLP fast weights are stored. The space and time complexity of novel-view rendering is therefore identical to that of TTT. We call our strategy Test-Time Baking (TTB), which can be viewed as generalized form of TTT. Formally, the fast-weight update rules of TTT and TTB are: θ(TTT) = θ ηθL(fθ(WkX), WvX), θ(TTB) = θ ηθL(fθ(WkX), g(X)), respectively, where θ is the fast weights of the MLP (), η and are the inner-loop learning rate and objective, Wk and Wv are linear projection matrices, and is the input tokens. The difference (6b) (6a) between TTT and TTB lies in the mapping target: WvX and g(X). In principle, we can employ an arbitrary function or tokens with additional modality for the mapping target g(X). Note that TTB falls back to TTT when X=X and is linear projection. In our case, we instantiate g() as the CrossAttn() from DVSM, which shifts TTB beyond the linear-attention interpretation [36] of TTT. Although this incurs additional reconstruction-time cost, once prefilled, rendering remains identical to TTT with substantially higher quality thanks to the enriched global information from g(). More analysis. We empirically validate that swapping the inner-loop target from WvX to CrossAttn(X) broadens the effective view field of the baked fast-weight MLP. At TTB block 7 with =16, we measure how much each context image contributes to the TTB output at the novelview rendering tokens via input-gradient saliency, sorted and averaged across output positions  (Fig. 4)  . The WvX variant peaks sharply at top-1 then decays, while CrossAttn(X) flattens the peak and sustains heavier mid-rank tail. This matches our design intent: CrossAttn(X) already aggregates across all context views, so each memorized pair inherits wider receptive field.

sections.title: 3.3.4 Fast-weight local-duplicate inference
sections.content: The baked fast weights have fixed capacity, causing quality to plateau as the number of context views grows. We address this at inference time by clustering the context views into spatially-local groups via k-means on per-view camera poses, with = /B for nominal budget of views per group. Each group is reconstructed independently by the unmodified model, so that cross-view attention and the inner-loop update only involve the views of that group, yielding per-group, per-layer fast weights {{θk,ℓ}L k=1. At rendering time, each novel view is routed to the group with the nearest centroid and queries only the corresponding copy. Rendering thus remains O(1) per view and each copy only has to absorb about views, while the stored state grows linearly with K. ℓ=1}K

sections.title: Implementation details
sections.content: We use 768 latent channels with 12 decoder blocks at patch size 8, replacing each cross-view attention with TTB layer. We initialize our models from the corresponding DVSM [58] checkpoint. We use AdamW [38] with cosine annealing and perceptual loss weight λ = 0.2. Models are trained on DL3DV-10K [35] dataset with 64 A100 GPUs. We first train at 340p for 100K iterations with learning rate 4104, then finetune at 480p, 720p, and 960p for 10K iterations each with learning rate 1105. We randomly sample either 16 or 32 context views per scene with the same number of target views. Ablations use smaller setup on 8 A100 GPUs at patch size 16 truncated to 720p, with efficiency metrics still reported at patch size 8 for consistency. sections.title: 4.3 Ablation studies
sections.content: From TTT to TTB. Tab. 4 decomposes the gap between vanilla LaCT-style TTT replacement [77] and our full TTB into three additive components: context pairing, switching to MSE with =3 inner steps (yielding TTB--), and replacing the linear-projection target with cross-view attention output. Each contributes meaningfully, and stacking all three closes the quality gap to DVSM [58] while retaining TTTs 50 FPS rendering. The reconstruction cost grows quadratically with due to the in-loop cross-view attention, consistent with our reconstruction time for rendering quality trade-off. Inner-loop optimization. Tab. 5 ablates the inner-loop loss and number of update steps . Switching from LaCTs unnormalized dot-product loss [77] to MSE consistently improves quality for both TTT and TTB--, with TTB-- benefiting more (+0.44 vs +0.27 PSNR). Increasing brings monotonic but diminishing gains, leading us to adopt =3 with MSE as sweet spot between quality and reconstruction cost. This asymmetric response aligns with our light field viewTTBs inner loop fits target function and benefits from convergence, while TTT-KVB is closer to one-shot linear write. TTB layer design. Tab. 6 ablates two design choices in our TTB layer. Residual learning reformulates the inner-loop target from the absolute cross-view attention output to its residual against (ctx-rend), reducing the magnitude of the regression target and easing the few-step inner-loop optimization. Feedback additionally applies the baked MLP to update the context ground-truth tokens, so that all three token streams propagate through identical operators in subsequent layers. Both designs contribute roughly equally in isolation (+0.43 and +0.44 PSNR) and combine to +0.52. Limitations. TTB is constrained by the fixed capacity of its fast-weight MLP, causing quality to saturate at large ; the local-duplicate routing that mitigates this is heuristic, and learning it during training is left for future work. Its inner-loop cross-view attention also makes reconstruction quadratic in , drawback for single-shot scenarios. Finally, TTB is built on reconstruction rather than generation, interpolating within context views without extrapolating to unobserved viewpoints.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We present Test-Time Baking (TTB), which retargets the TTT inner-loop optimization from raw value tokens to cross-view attention outputs, turning the fast-weight MLP from replacement for attention into its collaborator. Combined with context pair that resolves the reconstruction-rendering modality misalignment, TTB bakes DVSM-level scene information into fixed-size MLP while retaining TTT-level rendering complexity. Across DL3DV, Re10K, and in-the-wild benchmarks, TTB matches DVSM [58] quality at constant 23 FPS and consistently surpasses LaCT [77]. We hope this baking perspective offers new way to integrate attention and TTT beyond view synthesis.

sections.title: A Additional details
sections.content: A.1 Common implementation details Unless otherwise specified, all of our final models share the configuration described in this section. The decoder consists of 12 blocks with latent dimension of 768, organized as illustrated in main paper Fig. 3. Optimization is carried out with AdamW [38] using weight decay of 0.05 and momentum coefficients (0.9, 0.95). The learning rate is annealed along cosine schedule preceded by 2.5k linear warm-up iterations, peaking at 4104 during the lowest-resolution stage and dropping to 1105 when finetuning at higher resolutions. The perceptual term in our rendering loss is weighted by λ = 0.2. Training runs on 64 A100 GPUs, and we cast the learnable layers to BFloat16 mixed precision during forward propagation. Camera information is encoded with the Plücker parameterization [44]: each pixel is associated with 6-dimensional vector (ro rd, rd), where ro denotes the camera origin, rd the unit direction of the corresponding ray, and the vector cross product. We further normalize the context-view poses following the convention of GS-LRM [76]. Inside each transformer block, we adopt the pre-norm layout combined with QK-normalization. Each attention layer uses 12 heads, and every fully-connected sublayer expands the hidden dimension by factor of 4. All linear projections in our architecture are bias-free. A.2 TTB layer details This section elaborates on TTB layer details that were elided from the main paper for space. We provide the pseudocode of training our TTB model in Algo. 1 as complementary reference for the descriptions below. The three fast-weight matrices of our SwiGLU-MLP, w0, w2 RHdindh and w1 RHdhdout , are stored as ordinary learnable parameters and are jointly optimized in the outer loop alongside the rest of the network. Consequently, the inner loop for every scene starts from common, outer-loop-learned meta-initialization θ0, which is then advanced by Muon [28] update steps before being applied to the rendering tokens. When local-duplicate inference is enabled with > 1 groups, every per-group reconstruction starts from the same meta-initialized θ0 and is specialized only by the views assigned to its group, so all local copies share the same starting point and differ through their inner-loop trajectories. We initialize TTB models from the corresponding DVSM [58] checkpoint with strict=False: the patch embeddings, input LayerNorms, Plücker encoding, intra-view attention layers, both FFNs in each block, and the RGB head are inherited directly, while every module inside the TTB layerincluding its LayerNorm, query/key and value projections, output projection, per-token learning-rate head, output RMSNorm, and the fast weights w0, w1, w2is freshly initialized. The cross-view attention projections of DVSM are not reused, since the inner-loop target of TTB is structurally different and warm-starting from the DVSM projections did not yield benefits in our preliminary experiments. To prevent the random-init TTB layer from disrupting the inherited DVSM features at the start of finetuning, we initialize the TTB output projection with small standard deviation following the residual zero-init trick used in deep transformers, so that the TTB block contributes approximately zero at finetune step 0 and the entire forward pass reduces to the pretrained DVSM model plus an identity TTB layer. A.3 Two-view Re10K specific details For the two-view setting, each GPU receives 32 scenes per iteration, with 2 context views and 3 target views per scene. The interval between the two context frames is sampled uniformly between 25 and 192, and target frames are drawn from the union of all intermediate frames between the two context views and the extrapolated frames within 25 frames on either side. We initialize the model from the corresponding DVSM [58] Re10K checkpoint following the strategy detailed in Sec. A.2, and finetune it on Re10K for 100K iterations at 256256 followed by 10K iterations at 512512. Note that doubling the context tokens through the context pair (main paper Eq. 7) negligibly affects this two-view setup, so we keep the same per-GPU batch composition as DVSM. A.4 Many-view DL3DV [35] specific details DL3DV is the main benchmark for our dense-view results in main paper Tab. 1 and Tab. 3, as well as for all the ablations in main paper Sec. 4.3. For training, we adopt dynamic batching scheme that controls the per-GPU token budget rather than the number of scenes. Each scene draws either 16 or 32 context views uniformly at random, paired with the same number of target views; the number of scenes packed into GPU is then adjusted on the fly so that the aggregate count of context-pair tokens (i.e., the union of X(ctx-gt) and X(ctx-rend) across all scenes in the batch) stays within fixed budget. This compensates for the doubled token count introduced by the context pair and keeps the effective compute per iteration comparable to DVSM at the same memory ceiling. The frame interval between two adjacent context views is sampled uniformly from [1, 16], and target views are drawn from [min(C)2, max(C)+2] C, where is the index set of the sampled context views. We exclude from training small subset of scenes whose aspect ratio or native resolution does not match the canonical 16:9 960p layout. The resolution curriculum starts from 340p and runs for 100K iterations, after which the model is finetuned for 10K iterations at each of 480p, 720p, and the final 960p (540960). For the controlled ablation setting used in main paper Tab. 46 and Tab. 13, we shrink the compute footprint to 8 A100 GPUs by fixing the context view count to 32, raising the patch size to 16 to lower the per-token resolution, and truncating the curriculum to 340p / 480p / 720p with 100K / 10K / 10K iterations respectively. All the design knobs ablated in those tables share this controlled setup; the rendering and reconstruction efficiency reported alongside is measured on model with patch size 8 to remain consistent with the final main-table configuration. A.5 Zero-shot evaluation details The in-the-wild numbers in main paper Tab. 3 are produced by the DVSM-initialized 960p TTB model trained on DL3DV with patch size 8, evaluated zero-shot on three out-of-distribution datasets: the 9 scenes of MipNeRF360 [3], the 7 scenes of Free [66], and the 6 stable scenes from Hike [39] as identified by [33]. We hold out every 8th frame on MipNeRF360 and Free and every 10th frame on Hike as target views, and run k-means over the remaining frames to obtain context views. All input images are first resizedpreserving their original aspect ratioso that the total pixel count matches the 540960=518,400 target used by our model, and predicted novel views are then resized back to the datasets native resolution prior to metric computation. We apply the same image preprocessing pipeline to all baselines for fair comparison. The LagerNVS [61] numbers are produced from our intermediate 480p checkpoint, since LagerNVS operates at 512 pixels along the longer image side and matching its native input resolution is the cleanest comparison. A.6 Local-duplicate inference details This section gives further details of the local-duplicate inference described in main paper Sec. 3.3.4, which reconstructs the scene as spatially-local groups of context views at inference time, each with its own copy of the baked fast weights, so that single fast-weight MLP only has to absorb the views of one local group (about on average) instead of all views. It reuses the trained model as is, with no retraining and no additional learned parameters; the per-scene state grows to sets of fast weights. Grouping. Each context view is summarized into 6-dimensional descriptor fi = [ci; di] R6, where ci R3 is the camera origin and di R3 is the cameras unit optical axis, both expressed in the input world frame. The number of groups is an inference-time hyper-parameter; = 1 falls back to the single-MLP model. Unless stated otherwise we set = /B with nominal budget of = 16 views per group, i.e., = 2 for = 32 and = 4 for = 64. We then run Lloyds algorithm for 20 iterations with the Euclidean distance to cluster the descriptors into groups. Centroids are initialized with the descriptors of views whose indices are evenly spaced over [0, 1]; since our context views are ordered by capture time, this spreads the initial centroids along the camera trajectory. If centroid attracts no views during an iteration, we leave it unchanged for that round. Group sizes are neither balanced nor capped, and must stay small relative to . Per-group reconstruction. For every group we run the standard reconstruction pass of our model on its member views only. Inside this pass, all sublayersintra-view attention, FFN, cross-view attention, and the TTB inner loopsee only the tokens of group k; in particular, the cross-view attention that provides the baking target attends across the views of the group rather than across all views. The two streams (ctx-gt) and (ctx-rend) of context view are created inside the same pass and are therefore always baked together. Every pass starts from the shared meta-initialization θ0 and runs the same inner-loop steps, producing the per-layer fast weights {θk,ℓ}L ℓ=1 of copy k. The passes are independent of each other and are executed sequentially in our implementation. At the end of context prefilling we cache the fast weights of every group together with the cluster centroids. Rendering. At rendering time, we do not re-run k-means. Each novel view computes its own 6-dimensional descriptor in the same input world frame and takes an arg min of the Euclidean distance to the cached centroids to select single group, and all of its tokens are rendered with the fast weights of that group. The switch between copies is hard, without blending. The per-token rendering cost is unchanged and independent of ; routing only adds one nearest-centroid search over centroids per view, which is negligible. In our implementation every novel view is routed and rendered individually. sections.content: C.1 Few-view lower-resolution results We additionally train and evaluate our models on 2-view setup at lower resolution. This is not our intended scenario as the rendering FPS speedup by replacing cross-view attentions with our baked MLPs become marginal: 6472 at 256256 and 4552 at 512512. We follow previous works to train and test on Re10k [30] dataset. We start from the most capable pretrained checkpoint from DVSM [58] which employs DINO [52] injection and patch size of 8. We first train at 256256 resolution for 100K iterations with learning rate 4104, and then finetune at 512512 resolution for 10K iterations with learning rate 1104. In each iteration on GPU, we sample 32 scenes with 2 context views and 3 target views. The distance between the 2 views is randomly sampled between 25192 frame skips following previous works. The results comparison is presented in Tab. 16. Under such few views, our TTBs can faithfully reproduce the cross-view attentions results, as reflected by the comparable results with our pretrained DVSM. C.2 In-the-wild generalization at 16 input views We complement the 64-view in-the-wild evaluation in main paper Tab. 3 with 16-view counterpart in Tab. 10, covering the same three out-of-domain datasets (MipNeRF360 [3], Free [66], Hike [39]) at both 960p and 512-pixel longer-side settings. The trends mirror our in-domain DL3DV results: TTB closely matches DVSM [58] quality across all three datasets while consistently surpassing LaCT [77] and LVSM [25], and outperforms LagerNVS [61] by clear margin under the 512-pixel setting. Efficiency-wise, TTB retains its constant-FPS rendering at 16 views just as at 64 views, confirming that the rendering speedup is independent of context view count. These results indicate that TTBs quality and speed advantages generalize beyond the dense-view regime to fewer-view, out-of-domain scenarios. sections.title: D Qualitative results
sections.content: This section provides additional qualitative results that complement the quantitative comparisons in the main paper. We include in-domain comparisons on DL3DV [35] (Sec. D.1), two-view comparisons on Re10K [30] (Sec. D.2), and zero-shot comparisons on three in-the-wild datasets [3, 39, 66] (Sec. D.3). D.1 In-domain results on DL3DV Fig. 8 extends the comparison in main paper Fig. 5 to additional held-out DL3DV scenes spanning input view counts of =16, 32, and 64, complementing the three-column quantitative results in main paper Tab. 1. TTB consistently preserves thin geometric structures and high-frequency texture where LaCT [77] blurs and LVSM [25] loses detail. D.2 Two-view results on Re10K Fig. 9 compares TTB against DVSM [58] and LVSM [25] under the two-view setting, complementing main paper Tab. 2. TTB matches DVSMs quality at the same rendering speed-up regime, and outperforms LVSM in regions involving moderate viewpoint extrapolation. D.3 Zero-shot results on in-the-wild datasets Figs. 1012 report zero-shot results on MipNeRF360 [3], Free [66], and Hike [39], all using the DL3DV-trained TTB model with =64 input views. These figures complement the in-the-wild numerical results in main paper Tab. 3. Despite clear domain gap from DL3DV, TTB recovers fine details such as small text and thin structures that LaCT [77] and LVSM [25] blur out.

sections.title: E Broader impacts
sections.content: TTB shares its broader impacts with feed-forward novel-view synthesis methods in general. What is more specific to TTB is the methodological perspective it offers: rather than replacing attention with test-time-trained fast-weight MLP as in prior TTT-style architectures, TTB shows that the fast-weight MLP can be supervised to collaborate with attention by baking its outputs into constantsize state. Long-context language models, where attention KV-caches grow linearly with sequence length, could similarly benefit from baking attention outputs into fixed-capacity fast weight to enable constant-memory inference. World models and video generators that maintain long temporal context face the same memory-growth issue and may adopt analogous baking strategies for the temporal-attention component. Physical 3D perception systems that operate on streaming sensor inputs, such as embodied agents and autonomous driving stacks, could likewise use baked fastweight state to maintain compact running memory of the environment without unbounded KV growth. We hope the baking perspective inspires further exploration of how attention and test-time training can be combined across these domains.
